chapters.title: Chapter 1: Ancient Civilizations (Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Indus, and Chinese)

lessons.title: Mesopotamian Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
How We Know About the Past

Historians learn about ancient times from two kinds of sources. Primary sources are the original materials from the time of the event itself, such as inscriptions, coins, tools, weapons, buildings and official records; they give first-hand evidence. Secondary sources are written later by people who were not present, such as history books based on primary sources. Historians first study primary sources and then use secondary sources to understand and explain the past.

The Land and the Beginning

Mesopotamian Civilization grew between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates in present-day Iraq. It started in about 4500 BCE. The earliest people there were the Sumerians, who built city-states. Before the Babylonian Empire, the Akkadian Empire existed in Mesopotamia; founded by Sargon, it is considered the first empire of Mesopotamia. Later Hammurabi built the Babylonian Empire.

The Code of Hammurabi

The Code of Hammurabi was a set of 282 laws made by Hammurabi, the famous king of Babylon. The laws were carved on a large stone pillar so that everyone could see them. They covered trade, property, family, wages and punishments. Their main purpose was that people may respect each other and justice may prevail in society. It is one of the earliest written law codes of the world.

Trade, Architecture and Occupations

  • Trade: Mesopotamians exported grain, cloth and handicrafts and imported wood, stone, metals and ivory, using rivers and land routes.
  • Architecture: They built houses and palaces of mud-bricks and huge temple towers called ziggurats; their cities had planned streets.
  • Occupations: Most people were farmers who grew wheat, barley and dates with the help of irrigation canals; others were craftsmen, weavers, potters, metal workers, traders, priests, scribes and soldiers.

Key Points

  • Mesopotamian Civilization started in about 4500 BCE between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
  • Primary sources give first-hand evidence of the past; secondary sources are written later.
  • The Code of Hammurabi had 282 laws and is one of the earliest written law codes.
  • Ziggurats were the huge temple towers of Mesopotamia.

lessons.title: Egyptian Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
The Gift of the Nile

The River Nile was the lifeline of Egypt. Every year its flood left rich black silt on the banks, which made the land very fertile for growing wheat, barley and flax in an otherwise desert country. The Nile provided water for drinking and irrigation, fish for food, and an easy transport route for trade and communication. Because of the Nile, people settled on its banks, produced surplus food and built a great civilization — that is why Egypt is called the Gift of the Nile.

Social Structure

Egyptian society was divided into six classes: the Pharaoh (king) at the top; then the vizier, senior officials, high priest and nobles; then scribes; then skilled artisans and craftspeople; then peasant farmers and workers; and at the bottom, servants and slaves. The Pharaoh was the most influential person in the government.

Religion and Script

Egyptians worshipped many gods, such as the sun god Ra and the river god Hapy. They believed in life after death, so they preserved dead bodies as mummies and built pyramids as royal tombs. Mummification began by about 2600 BCE. A pyramid had three chambers for different purposes connected with the king's burial and treasures. Their script was hieroglyphic, made of picture signs, written on stone and on papyrus paper. They also made progress in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and calendar making.

Famous Pharaohs

Tutankhamun was a young pharaoh who became king at about nine years of age (around 1332 BCE) and died in his teens. He is world famous because his tomb in the Valley of the Kings was discovered almost intact in 1922 by Howard Carter, filled with golden treasures including his famous gold mask. Cleopatra, the last famous ruler of Egypt, was born in Egypt and ruled it as queen, but by descent she was Greek (Macedonian), of the Ptolemaic dynasty founded by a general of Alexander the Great. She learned the Egyptian language and adopted Egyptian customs and religion.

Key Points

  • Egypt is called the Gift of the Nile because the river made farming and life possible there.
  • Egyptian society had six classes, with the Pharaoh at the top.
  • Egyptians used the hieroglyphic script and preserved the dead as mummies.
  • Tutankhamun's tomb was found almost intact in 1922 by Howard Carter.

lessons.title: Indus Valley Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
Mehrgarh — The Beginning

Mehrgarh, in the Kacchi Plain near the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, is one of the oldest known farming settlements in the world, dating back to about 7000 BCE. Its people were among the first to grow crops like wheat and barley and to domesticate animals such as goats, sheep and cattle. With time they built mud-brick houses, made pottery, tools of stone and bone, ornaments of shell and semi-precious stones, and stored grain in granaries. Mehrgarh shows the change of humans from hunters to farmers, and it laid the foundation for the later Indus Valley Civilization.

Role of the River Indus

The River Indus and its tributaries provided water for drinking, farming and animals, which attracted people to settle on its plains. Its yearly floods left fertile soil for growing wheat, barley, cotton and other crops, producing surplus food that supported large cities. The river also served as a trade route, connecting Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa with each other and with distant lands. These were the two main city cultures of the civilization: Mohenjo-Daro in Sindh on the Indus, and Harappa in Punjab on the Ravi.

Characteristics of the Civilization

  • Daily life: Well-planned cities with straight streets, baked-brick houses, covered drains and great baths; people wore cotton clothes and ornaments of gold, silver and beads.
  • Agriculture: Wheat, barley, peas, dates and cotton were grown; buffaloes, goats and sheep were domesticated.
  • Trade: Trade with Mesopotamia and other regions; cotton, beads and pottery were exported, and standard weights and measures were used.
  • Religion: Worship of a mother goddess and a male god (proto-Shiva), and of sacred animals and trees.
  • Script: A pictographic script, found mostly on small stone seals, generally written from right to left; it has still not been deciphered.

Decline of the Civilization

Historians suggest several causes for the end of the Indus Valley Civilization (around 1900–1500 BCE): repeated floods and changes in the course of rivers, the drying up of rivers and climate change reducing rainfall, decline in trade with Mesopotamia, overuse of land, and possibly invasions by new peoples such as the Aryans. Most probably a combination of natural changes made the great cities unsustainable, and people gradually left them. The civilization is also remembered for its terracotta toys — toy carts with wheels, bulls, monkeys, birds, whistles and rattles found at Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa.

Key Points

  • Mehrgarh (about 7000 BCE) in Balochistan is one of the world's earliest farming settlements.
  • Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa were the two great cities of the Indus Valley Civilization.
  • The Indus script is pictographic and has not been deciphered yet.
  • Changing rivers and a drier climate were the main causes of the civilization's decline.

lessons.title: Chinese Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
Basic Characteristics

Ancient Chinese Civilization grew in the river valleys of China. Silk was discovered in China in about 2700 BCE, and silk became its most valuable product. Society included farmers, silk weavers, potters, craftsmen, traders, soldiers and government officials called mandarins, who were selected through examinations.

Chinese Architecture

Buildings were mostly made of wood and mud-bricks with tiled, sloping roofs that turned up at the corners. Palaces and temples were built on raised platforms, and great emphasis was placed on symmetry and balance. The Great Wall of China is the most famous example of their building skill. It was ordered to be built by the Chinese Emperor Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of united China (about 221 BCE), who joined and extended the earlier walls to protect China from the invasions of northern tribes. Later dynasties continued to repair and extend it.

Trade and Occupations

China traded silk, tea, porcelain (china clay pottery) and paper through the famous Silk Road to Central Asia and Europe; silk was the most valuable export. Most people were farmers growing rice, wheat and tea; others were silk weavers, potters, craftsmen, traders, soldiers and government officials.

Gifts of Ancient China to the World

Ancient China's gifts still shape the modern world: paper and printing made books and knowledge cheap and widespread; gunpowder changed warfare and is used in fireworks; the magnetic compass made sea travel and navigation possible; and silk and porcelain remain prized goods. Chinese inventions like the wheelbarrow and tea cultivation also spread through the Silk Road and impact our daily life even today.

Key Points

  • Silk was discovered in China in about 2700 BCE.
  • The Great Wall was ordered by Emperor Qin Shi Huang to stop northern invasions.
  • China exported silk, tea, porcelain and paper through the Silk Road.
  • Paper, printing, gunpowder and the magnetic compass are China's gifts to the world.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Persian, Greek and Roman Civilizations

lessons.title: Persian Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
Cyrus the Great — Founder of the Empire

The Persian Empire was founded in 550 BCE by Cyrus the Great. He was a wise and tolerant ruler who conquered Media, Lydia and Babylon and united a vast empire. He is remembered for respecting the religions and customs of the conquered peoples and for freeing the Jews from Babylonian captivity.

How the Empire Was Organized

Cyrus's successors organized the empire with provinces called satrapies, each ruled by a satrap, with royal inspectors to watch them, and a network of roads and messengers. Society was headed by the king, followed by nobles, priests, soldiers, merchants, craftsmen and farmers. Politically, Persia was a centralized empire: one king ruled vast lands through satraps, valuing order, loyalty and tolerance of different peoples' customs.

Expansion Over Three Older Civilizations

The Persian Empire expanded over the lands of three major older civilizations: the Mesopotamian (Babylonian) civilization — Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BCE; the Egyptian civilization — conquered by Cambyses in 525 BCE; and the Indus Valley region — the empire extended up to the Indus. In this way Persia became heir to the oldest civilizations of the world.

Persian Architecture and Decline

Persian architecture showed royal grandeur: grand palaces like Persepolis with huge columned halls, tall pillars with animal capitals, wide staircases and glazed-brick reliefs, designed to show the emperor's power. Persians and Greeks were similar in believing in gods connected with nature and sky, building grand temples and palaces with columns, and valuing art and strong armies. The empire declined because of weak later kings, revolts of provinces and heavy taxes, and finally Alexander's invasion ended it: he began the conquest in 334 BCE, winning at Granicus, Issus (333 BCE) and Gaugamela (331 BCE) against Darius III.

Key Points

  • Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire in 550 BCE.
  • The empire was divided into provinces called satrapies, ruled by satraps.
  • Persia expanded over Babylonian, Egyptian and Indus lands.
  • Alexander ended the Persian Empire with victories at Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela.

lessons.title: Greek Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
City-States: Athens and Sparta

Greek Civilization developed in independent city-states (polis) such as Athens and Sparta around the Aegean Sea. A shared language, religion and games united them culturally, though they remained politically separate. Athens was famous for democracy, education, art and philosophy, while Sparta was a military state famous for its discipline and powerful army. Their rivalry led to the Peloponnesian War in 431 BCE, when war broke out between Athens and the Spartans.

Daily and Political Life

In Athens, male citizens took part directly in the assembly (democracy), debated in the Agora and served on juries; in Sparta, society was organized for military training. The Agora was the central public place of a Greek city-state: a marketplace where goods were bought and sold, and a gathering place where citizens met and discussed politics; important public buildings and temples were often built around it. Social life included festivals, theatre and the Olympic Games. Plato's Academy in Athens was like a school, where philosophy was taught.

The Olympic Games

The Olympic Games were athletic competitions held in ancient Greece at Olympia in honour of the god Zeus, beginning in 776 BCE and held every four years. Athletes from Greek city-states competed in running, wrestling, discus and other events, and wars were paused during the games. They were revived in the late 19th century (1896) as the modern Olympic Games, now the world's biggest sports event.

Alexander the Great

Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE), king of Macedonia, conquered in about twelve years the largest empire of the ancient world, from Greece to Egypt and Persia and up to the Indus Valley. He wanted to conquer the world out of ambition for rule and glory and a love of adventure; he was also attracted by the wealth of India. His Indian campaign began in 327 BCE; he defeated King Porus at the Jhelum but treated him generously, and stopped when his tired soldiers refused to go further. Greek architecture is famous for beautiful marble temples like the Parthenon, with elegant columns of three orders — Doric, Ionic and Corinthian. Greek civilization declined because its city-states constantly fought each other, until Macedonia and then Rome conquered them.

Key Points

  • Athens stood for democracy and learning; Sparta for military discipline.
  • The Agora was the marketplace and meeting place of a Greek city-state.
  • The Olympic Games began in 776 BCE and were revived in 1896.
  • Alexander conquered from Greece to the Indus in about twelve years.

lessons.title: Roman Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
From Kingdom to Republic

Roman Civilization began with the city of Rome in Italy in 753 BCE. Rome was first ruled by kings. The last king, Tarquin, was harsh and unpopular, so in 509 BCE the Romans expelled him and decided never to have a king again. They set up a republic, in which power was shared: two consuls elected for one year headed the government, the Senate advised and made important decisions, and assemblies of citizens voted on laws and elected officials. Over time the common people (plebeians) also won rights, including their own representatives called tribunes. This republican system governed Rome for about 500 years, and later Rome became an empire ruling the whole Mediterranean world.

Roman Society and Life

Roman society was divided into patricians (rich nobles) and plebeians (common people), with slaves at the bottom. Citizens voted in assemblies and were governed by the Senate and elected officials in the republic. Romans enjoyed public baths, forums and games in amphitheatres like the Colosseum, a huge amphitheatre in the centre of Rome.

Greeks and Romans

Greeks and Romans had close and long relations. After conquering Greece (by 146 BCE), Greece became part of the Roman world. The Romans greatly admired Greek culture: they adopted Greek gods (with Roman names), art, architecture, literature and education. In return, Rome gave Greece peace, roads, Roman law and citizenship. That is why Roman civilization is often called Greco-Roman — conquered Greece conquered its Roman conquerors culturally.

Roman Architecture and Decline

Roman architecture was practical and engineering-based: Romans used arches, domes and concrete to build huge structures like the Colosseum, aqueducts, roads, bridges and baths. In short, Persians showed royal grandeur, Greeks showed beauty and harmony, and Romans showed engineering strength and utility. The Roman Empire declined due to weak and corrupt emperors, a too-large empire difficult to govern, economic problems, attacks by Germanic tribes and internal civil wars; the western Roman Empire finally fell in 476 CE.

Key Points

  • Rome began in 753 BCE and became a republic in 509 BCE.
  • Two consuls, the Senate and citizens' assemblies shared power in the republic.
  • Romans adopted Greek culture, so their civilization is called Greco-Roman.
  • Roman architecture used arches, domes and concrete; the western empire fell in 476 CE.

lessons.title: The Aryans
lessons.notes_html:
Origin of the Aryans

The Aryans are believed to have originated in Central Asia, in the steppes around the Caspian region. The term 'Arya' means noble. They were herders and warriors who spoke an early form of Sanskrit. Around 1500 BCE, groups of Aryans migrated eastward, entering the north-western parts of the subcontinent through mountain passes such as the Khyber Pass, and settled first in the Punjab — the land of rivers, Sapta Sindhu. Gradually they spread over the Ganga valley, cleared forests, settled as farmers, and composed the Vedas, our main source about their early life.

Structure of Aryan Society

Aryan society was organized under the caste (varna) system, which divided people into four castes:

  • Brahmins — priests and teachers who performed religious duties and preserved the Vedas.
  • Kshatriyas — kings and warriors who ruled and defended.
  • Vaishyas — farmers, herders and traders.
  • Shudras — labourers and servants who served the other three.

In the early period caste was based on work, but later it became hereditary and rigid. The family was patriarchal, headed by the father; people lived mostly in villages, and assemblies like the Sabha and Samiti helped the chief (rajan). The main source of wealth of the Aryans was cattle: cows gave milk, food and status, and wealth was counted in cattle; later agriculture also became important.

Religious Beliefs of the Aryans

The early Aryans worshipped the forces of nature as gods: Indra (rain and war), Agni (fire), Surya (sun), Vayu (wind), Varuna (sky and moral order) and Ushas (dawn). They performed yajnas (fire sacrifices) and offered soma juice and food to the gods, singing hymns collected in the Rigveda. There were no temples or idols in the earliest period; prayers were offered in the open. Over time, rituals became complex, priests gained importance, and ideas of karma, rebirth and the soul (atman) developed in the Upanishads.

Key Points

  • The Aryans came from Central Asia and settled first in the Punjab (Sapta Sindhu).
  • 'Arya' means noble; Aryan society had four castes based originally on work.
  • Cattle were the main source of Aryan wealth.
  • The Aryans worshipped nature gods and composed the Vedas.

lessons.title: The Mauryan Empire
lessons.notes_html:
Rise of the Mauryan Dynasty

The Mauryan Dynasty was founded by Chandragupta Maurya in 321 BCE, who, with the help of his wise minister Chanakya (Kautilya), overthrew the Nanda dynasty and united most of India for the first time. The Maurya Empire fully occupied the north-western parts of India by 316 BCE. His son Bindusara and grandson Ashoka expanded the empire until it stretched from Afghanistan to Bengal and from the Himalayas to the Deccan. The empire lasted from 321 to 185 BCE.

Contributions of the Mauryas

  • A strong centralized administration and a spy system.
  • A well-organized army and revenue system.
  • Chanakya's book Arthashastra, a famous work on statecraft.
  • Ashoka's policy of Dhamma, welfare works and the spread of Buddhism to Central and South-East Asia.
  • Fine art and architecture, such as the Lion Capital and rock edicts.

Key Points

  • Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire in 321 BCE with Chanakya's help.
  • The Mauryas united most of India for the first time.
  • Chanakya wrote the Arthashastra on statecraft.
  • The empire stretched from Afghanistan to Bengal at its greatest extent.

lessons.title: Ashoka and His Dhamma
lessons.notes_html:
Life of Ashoka

Ashoka (ruled 268–232 BCE) was the grandson of Chandragupta Maurya and the greatest Mauryan emperor. He became emperor of the Mauryan Empire in 268 BCE. In the early part of his reign he expanded the empire, but the bloody Kalinga War (about 261 BCE) changed his life: seeing the terrible bloodshed, suffering and deaths of thousands filled him with sorrow and remorse. He gave up wars of conquest, embraced Buddhism, and adopted Dhamma — conquest by righteousness instead of by the sword.

What Was Dhamma?

Dhamma was a code of morality teaching respect for parents and elders, kindness to servants and animals, tolerance of all religions and non-violence. Ashoka engraved his edicts on rocks and polished stone pillars across the empire so that everyone could read his message.

Why His Period Is a Golden Era

Ashoka's period is called a golden era because after the Kalinga War he devoted his rule to the welfare of his people. He built hospitals, roads, wells and rest houses, planted trees along roads, protected animals, and sent missions of Buddhism to other countries, including Sri Lanka and Central Asia. His empire enjoyed peace, justice and prosperity, and he ruled it peacefully for about 40 years. His famous art includes the Lion Capital at Sarnath, now India's national emblem.

Why Ashoka Was Forgotten for So Long

Ashoka remained unknown for a long time because his edicts were written in the Brahmi script, which people forgot how to read after his empire ended. For nearly two thousand years no one could read his inscriptions. Only in the 19th century (1837) did James Prinsep decipher the Brahmi script; historians could then read the edicts and discover that 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' of the pillars was actually Emperor Ashoka.

Key Points

  • Ashoka became emperor in 268 BCE; the Kalinga War (261 BCE) changed his life.
  • He gave up conquest by the sword and adopted Dhamma — conquest by righteousness.
  • He built hospitals, roads, wells and rest houses and spread Buddhism abroad.
  • James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837 and revealed Ashoka to history.

lessons.title: The Kushans and the Guptas
lessons.notes_html:
The Kushan Era

The Kushans were a Central Asian tribe who built a large empire in the 1st–3rd centuries CE covering Central Asia and north-western India, with capitals at Peshawar (Purushapura) and Mathura. Their greatest king, Kanishka (from 78 CE), was a patron of Buddhism: he held a Buddhist council and sent missionaries who spread Buddhism along the Silk Route into China. The era is famous for flourishing trade on the Silk Route between China, India and Rome, gold coins of fine quality, and religious tolerance and prosperity in the region of present-day Pakistan.

Gandhara Art

Gandhara Art flourished in the Gandhara region (the present-day Peshawar valley and surroundings) under the patronage of the Kushan kings, especially Kanishka. Because the Kushan Empire stood where Greek, Roman, Persian and Indian cultures met, its artists combined Greek-Roman techniques with Buddhist subjects — producing the first human images of Buddha with wavy hair and draped robes like Greek statues. Monasteries at places like Taxila and Takht-i-Bahi were centres of this art.

The Gupta Empire — A Golden Age

The first ruler of the Gupta Empire was Chandragupta-I, who founded the empire around 320 CE and started the Gupta Era. His son Samudragupta and grandson Chandragupta-II expanded it into a great power. The Gupta period was prosperous: agriculture flourished, foreign trade brought wealth, towns and markets were busy, and fine gold coins show the empire's economic strength — that is why this age is called the Golden Age of India. Gupta society followed the four-caste system strictly, while Kushan society was more mixed and cosmopolitan, with many languages and religions living side by side along the Silk Route.

Gupta Mathematics and the Barter Problem

The Gupta age gave great gifts to mathematics: Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya (499 CE) and gave the value of pi (3.1416); the concept of zero as a number and the decimal place-value system were developed in India in this era and spread to the world. Trade in early times also faced the problems of the barter system — exchanging goods directly: each person had to find someone who wanted exactly what he had (double coincidence of wants), there was no common measure of value, goods could not be divided easily or stored if perishable. These problems led people to adopt money.

Key Points

  • Kanishka, the greatest Kushan king, patronized Buddhism and Gandhara Art.
  • Chandragupta-I founded the Gupta Empire around 320 CE.
  • The Gupta age is called the Golden Age of India.
  • Zero, the decimal system and Aryabhata's astronomy are Gupta-age gifts.

lessons.title: Life of Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him)
lessons.notes_html:
Early Life

Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) was born in Makkah in 571 CE, the Year of the Elephant. His father Abdullah had died before his birth, and his mother Amina died when he was six, so he was raised by his grandfather and then his uncle Abu Talib. He became famous for honesty and was called Al-Amin (the Trustworthy). At 25 he married Hazrat Khadija (RA). At the age of 40 (610 CE) he received the first revelation in Cave Hira and began preaching Islam.

From Makkah to Medina

For thirteen years in Makkah he patiently invited people to worship one Allah, enduring persecution without violence. Tired of the Makkans' oppression, some Muslims had already migrated around 615 CE to Abyssinia (Ethiopia). In 622 CE the Prophet (peace be upon him) migrated to Medina — the Hijrah — where he founded the first Islamic state, built Masjid-e-Nabvi as the centre of the community, and made agreements with other tribes.

Role in Spreading Islam

He spread Islam first by his own character and preaching. In Medina he sent letters and delegations inviting the rulers of Persia, Rome (Byzantium), Egypt and Abyssinia to Islam. Through his teachings, his example of justice, honesty and mercy, and the training of his companions, Islam spread throughout Arabia in his lifetime. The main events of the Medina period include the Battles of Badr, Uhud and Khandaq, the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the peaceful conquest of Makkah (630 CE) and the Farewell Pilgrimage (632 CE), in which he delivered his famous last sermon on the equality of mankind, the rights of women and the sanctity of life and property. He passed away in Medina in 632 CE.

Key Points

  • Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) was born in Makkah in 571 CE and was known as Al-Amin.
  • The first revelation came in Cave Hira in 610 CE.
  • The Hijrah to Medina in 622 CE founded the first Islamic state and started the Islamic calendar.
  • He conquered Makkah peacefully in 630 CE and delivered the Farewell Sermon in 632 CE.

lessons.title: Battles of Islam and the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
lessons.notes_html:
The Battle of Badr (624 CE)

The Battle of Badr was the first great battle of Islam, fought in 624 CE between 313 Muslims led by the Prophet (peace be upon him) and about 1,000 Quraysh of Makkah. Despite being few and poorly equipped, the Muslims won a decisive victory through faith, discipline and Allah's help. Many leading enemies were killed, and the victory established the Muslims as a strong power in Arabia.

The Battle of Uhud (625 CE)

The Battle of Uhud was fought in 625 CE (3 AH), a year after Badr, at Mount Uhud near Medina. The Quraysh came with a large army to take revenge for Badr. The Muslims fought bravely but suffered heavy losses — including the martyrdom of Hazrat Hamza (RA) — when some archers left their post against orders. The battle taught the Muslims the importance of complete obedience to the Prophet (peace be upon him).

The Battle of Khandaq — the Trench (627 CE)

In the Battle of Khandaq (627 CE), a confederacy of about 10,000 men besieged Medina. On the advice of Hazrat Salman Farsi (RA), the Muslims dug a deep trench around the open side of the city, which the enemy cavalry could not cross. After a long siege, hunger, cold winds and divisions forced the enemy to withdraw. Outcomes: Makkah's power to attack Medina was broken forever, the prestige of the Muslims rose, and the initiative passed to the Muslims.

The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628 CE)

The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628 CE / 6 AH) was a peace treaty between the Muslims of Medina and the Quraysh of Makkah, signed when the Muslims were stopped from performing Umrah. Its terms included a ten-year truce, the Muslims returning that year and performing Umrah the next year, and freedom for tribes to ally with either side. Although it looked unfavourable, it proved a 'clear victory': Islam spread rapidly in the peace that followed, and it paved the way for the conquest of Makkah.

Key Points

  • At Badr (624 CE), 313 Muslims defeated about 1,000 Quraysh.
  • At Uhud (625 CE), the archers leaving their post caused heavy Muslim losses.
  • At Khandaq (627 CE), a trench dug on Salman Farsi's advice saved Medina.
  • The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628 CE) brought ten years of peace and rapid spread of Islam.

lessons.title: The Rashidun Caliphs
lessons.notes_html:
Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddiq (RA) — The First Caliph

Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddiq (RA) (632–634 CE), the first Caliph, saved the Islamic state at its most dangerous moment. He faced severe challenges: false prophets like Musaylima arose claiming prophethood; many tribes rebelled and refused to pay zakat; and the empires of Persia and Rome threatened the borders. He met all these with firmness and faith: he fought the Ridda wars, enforced zakat, kept the state united, had the Holy Quran collected in book form, and sent armies towards Iraq and Syria, opening the way for Islam to spread beyond Arabia.

Hazrat Umar Bin Khattab (RA) — The Second Caliph

Hazrat Umar Bin Khattab (RA) (634–644 CE) was the second Rashid Caliph. Under him Islam spread rapidly: Persia (Iraq and Iran), Syria, Palestine and Egypt came under Muslim rule. He organized the state with departments, courts, a calendar (Hijri) and stipends, and ruled with famous justice, so people of conquered lands welcomed Muslim rule and Islam spread widely and peacefully.

Hazrat Usman Ghani (RA) — The Third Caliph

Hazrat Usman Ghani (RA) remained Caliph for about twelve years, from 644 CE to 656 CE. During his caliphate the Islamic state expanded greatly and the navy was established. His greatest service was the compilation of the authentic, standard copy of the Holy Quran, sent to all provinces — that is why he is called Jami-ul-Quran (compiler of the Quran). His martyrdom in 656 CE was the first great internal tragedy of the Muslim community: disagreement over bringing his killers to justice led to conflicts during the caliphate of Hazrat Ali (RA), and the unity of the caliphate was shaken.

Hazrat Ali (RA) — The Fourth Caliph

Hazrat Ali (RA), the fourth Caliph, remained Caliph for about five years. His caliphate faced the conflicts that followed the martyrdom of Hazrat Usman (RA), including the battles of Jamal and Siffin. The four Rashidun Caliphs together ruled for about thirty years and carried Islam from Arabia into Persia, Syria, Palestine and Egypt.

Key Points

  • Abu Bakr (RA) united Arabia through the Ridda wars and compiled the Quran in book form.
  • Umar (RA), the second caliph, organized the state and saw Islam reach Persia, Syria and Egypt.
  • Usman (RA) ruled about twelve years and prepared the standard copy of the Quran — Jami-ul-Quran.
  • Ali (RA), the fourth caliph, remained caliph for about five years.

mcqs.q: Hazrat Umar Bin Khattab (RA) was the Rashid Caliph:
mcqs.why: Hazrat Umar Bin Khattab (RA) was the second Rashid Caliph (634–644 CE), after Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddiq (RA).

mcqs.q: Hazrat Ali (RA) remained Caliph for:
mcqs.why: Hazrat Ali (RA), the fourth Caliph, remained Caliph for about five years, as given in the book.

mcqs.q: The first Caliph of Islam was:
mcqs.why: Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddiq (RA) (632–634 CE) was the first Caliph, who saved the Islamic state at its most dangerous moment.

mcqs.q: The wars fought by Abu Bakr (RA) against false prophets and rebellious tribes are called:
mcqs.why: Abu Bakr (RA) fought the Ridda (apostasy) wars against false prophets like Musaylima and tribes that refused zakat, and reunited Arabia within two years.

mcqs.q: Abu Bakr (RA) had the Holy Quran:
mcqs.why: Among Abu Bakr's (RA) great services, he had the Holy Quran collected in book form to preserve it after many memorizers were martyred in battle.

mcqs.q: Under Hazrat Umar (RA), which regions came under Muslim rule?
mcqs.why: Under Umar (RA), Islam spread rapidly: Persia (Iraq and Iran), Syria, Palestine and Egypt came under Muslim rule.

mcqs.q: Hazrat Umar (RA) organized the state by introducing:
options: Departments, courts, the Hijri calendar and stipends
mcqs.why: Umar (RA) organized the state with departments, courts, a calendar (Hijri) and stipends, and ruled with famous justice.

mcqs.q: Hazrat Usman Ghani (RA) remained Caliph for about:
mcqs.why: Hazrat Usman Ghani (RA) remained Caliph for about twelve years, from 644 CE to 656 CE (23–35 AH).

mcqs.q: Hazrat Usman (RA) is called Jami-ul-Quran because he:
options: Compiled the authentic, standard copy of the Holy Quran
Wrote a commentary of the Quran
mcqs.why: Usman's (RA) greatest service was the compilation of the authentic, standard copy of the Holy Quran, sent to all provinces — hence his title Jami-ul-Quran.

mcqs.q: An impact of the martyrdom of Hazrat Usman (RA) was:
options: Internal strife (fitna) and conflicts during Hazrat Ali's (RA) caliphate
mcqs.why: Usman's martyrdom in 656 CE opened the door to civil strife; disagreement over his killers led to the battles of Jamal and Siffin in Ali's (RA) caliphate and shook the unity of the caliphate.
